claim: iTregs show stronger suppression than tTregs on OT-II proliferation in response to epitope peptide loaded DCs.
source: We found that in vitro iTregs show stronger suppression than tTregs on OT-II proliferation in response to epitope peptide loaded DCs (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A comparing suppressive activity between tTreg and iTreg.

claim: iTregs possess stronger binding force to DCs than tTregs.
source: In accordance with the stronger suppression, single-cell force spectroscopy analysis showed that iTregs possessed apparent binding to DCs, even stronger than tTregs (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by single-cell force spectroscopy measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: iTregs show increased binding force compared with activated Tconvs.
source: In addition, iTregs also showed increased binding force compared with activated Tconvs (Figure 1C), suggesting the strong binding force is a common feature of both types of Tregs, but not Tconvs.
evidence: Supported by force spectroscopy data in Figure 1C comparing iTregs with activated Tconvs.

claim: The protein-level expression of Foxp3 reached its peak on day 2 after iTreg induction.
source: We measured the expression of Foxp3 more precisely, and noticed that the protein-level expression of Foxp3 reached its peak on day 2 after the induction (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by time-course measurements of Foxp3 expression shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Basal Ca2+ oscillation in treated Tconvs was gradually diminished during iTreg induction, with Foxp3 accumulation leading this by roughly 1 day.
source: With the accumulation of Foxp3 protein, basal Ca2+ oscillation in the treated Tconvs was gradually diminished, with the former leading the latter roughly by 1 day (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by time-course calcium oscillation measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The transcription level of Ryr2 was suppressed both in iTregs and tTregs.
source: As expected, the transcription level of Ryr2 was suppressed both in iTregs and tTregs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that the strong binding force with DC may come from reduced calcium oscillation as a result of Foxp3-mediated suppression of Ryr2 transcription.
evidence: Supported by QPCR data for Ryr2 mRNA expression shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The induction efficiency of Foxp3 was not affected by Ryr2 knock out.
source: While Ryr2 expression may be regulated by Foxp3, the induction efficiency of Foxp3 was not affected by Ryr2 knock out (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing Foxp3 induction in Ryr2 knockout versus control mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TCR signaling leads to a dramatic reduction of Foxp3+ cells in iTregs, but not in tTregs.
source: It was reported previously that TCR signaling led to a dramatic reduction of Foxp3+ cells in iTregs, but not in tTregs (Chen et al., 2011; Selvaraj and Geiger, 2007). We reproduced these data in our laboratory (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and cited references (Chen et al., 2011; Selvaraj and Geiger, 2007).

claim: tTregs have been reported to show an attenuated response to TCR triggering.
source: tTregs have been reported to show an attenuated response to TCR triggering (Sumpter et al., 2008; Vaeth et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2015), the exact point of signal attenuation in tTregs has not been elucidated.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Sumpter et al., 2008; Vaeth et al., 2012; Yan et al., 2015).

claim: SOCE activation is by far the strongest Ca2+ event in T cells.
source: As the extracellular Ca2+ is roughly 4 logs higher than the intracellular, SOCE activation is by far the strongest Ca2+ event in T cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and is also distinct from the other Ca2+ signaling patterns for its persistent vibration lasting hours to days (Christo et al., 2015; Wülfing et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and cited references (Christo et al., 2015; Wülfing et al., 1997).

claim: iTregs lost Foxp3 at the lowest dose of anti-CD3/CD28 required to activate, yet tTregs were resistant to an eightfold increase in both.
source: We titrated anti CD3/CD28 concentrations, and iTregs lost Foxp3 at the lowest dose required to activate, yet tTregs were resistant to an eightfold increase in both (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The first wave of SOCE in iTregs was slightly higher than Tconvs and tTregs, but there was no discernable difference between tTregs and Tconvs.
source: To study the molecular basis for the weak response in tTregs, we first monitored the early SOCE intensity in iTregs and tTregs, we found the first wave of SOCE in iTregs was slightly higher than Tconvs and tTregs, but there was no discernable difference between tTregs and Tconvs (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry measurements of early SOCE shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The phosphorylation of CD3ζ was similar in Tconv and nTreg immediately after TCR crosslink.
source: In addition, the phosphorylation of CD3ζ was similar in Tconv and nTreg immediately after TCR crosslink (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data for pCD3ζ shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In Tconvs and iTregs, Ca2+ remained cyclic waves expected in SOCE pulsation, but this Ca2+ signal was suddenly lost in tTregs 40–50 min after activation.
source: In Tconvs and iTregs, Ca2+ remained cyclic waves expected in SOCE pulsation. In contrast, this Ca2+ signal was suddenly lost in tTregs 40–50 min after the activation (Figure 2C; Videos 1–3).
evidence: Supported by long-term calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C and Videos 1-3.

claim: In contrast to iTregs and Tconvs, tTregs' NFATc1 and c2 failed to translocate into the nucleus.
source: In contrast to other transcriptional factors, such as NF-κB, activated rapidly in response to short Ca2+ elevation, NFATs are known to be triggered only by sustained cytoplasmic Ca2+ (Dolmetsch et al., 1998; Dolmetsch et al., 1997; Tomida et al., 2003). Indeed, in contrast to iTregs and Tconvs, tTregs' NFATc1 and c2 failed to translocate into the nucleus (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data showing nuclear/cytoplasmic NFAT distribution in Figure 2D and cited references (Dolmetsch et al., 1998; Dolmetsch et al., 1997; Tomida et al., 2003).

claim: In iTregs, anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation led a quick drop in cytoplasmic NFAT in 2 hr, with moderate accumulation of NFAT in the nucleus.
source: Upon detailed analysis, in iTregs, anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation led a quick drop in cytoplasmic NFAT in 2 hr, with moderate accumulation of NFAT in the nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by time-course western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: tTregs are known to have reduced NFAT activation in response to TCR ligation.
source: While tTregs are known to have reduced NFAT activation in response to TCR ligation (Sumpter et al., 2008; Nayak et al., 2009), our results pointed to a truncated Ca2+ response likely to be the molecular basis for this phenotype.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Sumpter et al., 2008; Nayak et al., 2009).

claim: Some tTregs treated with TG lost their Foxp3.
source: As expected, some tTregs treated with TG lost their Foxp3 (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Foxp3 expression in TG-treated tTregs in Figure 3E (note: this is Figure 2E in the text).

claim: The truncated Ca2+ in tTregs is essential to protect tTregs from phenotypical shift.
source: These results collectively argue that the truncated Ca2+ in tTregs is essential to protect tTregs from phenotypical shift.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results showing that forced calcium signal destabilizes tTregs.

claim: Tconvs were quite different before and after activation, but the changes of tTregs before and after TCR activation were more limited compared with Tconvs.
source: In RNA-seq data, principal component analysis (PCA) and heatmap of DEG (differentially expressed gene analysis) indicated that Tconvs were quite different before and after activation, but the changes of tTregs before and after TCR activation were more limited compared with Tconvs (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), verifying that tTregs have low TCR responsiveness.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq PCA and DEG analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: iTregs acquired partial Treg features after induction, shown as an intermediate between Tconvs and tTregs on PC2.
source: Comparing the transcriptome characteristics with other cell types, iTregs acquired partial Treg features after induction, shown as an intermediate between Tconvs and tTregs on PC2 (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Among all cell states, iTregs had the highest PC1 scores, representing higher proliferation state, probably due to the 4 days of induction.
source: While among all cell states, iTregs had the highest PC1 scores, represent higher proliferation state, probably due to the 4 days of induction (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, with speculation about the cause.

claim: In the PCA plot of ATAC-seq data, tTregs showed fewer changes after activation compared to Tconvs, while iTregs were closer to activated Tconv cells.
source: Next, we analyzed the chromatin accessibility of these cells using ATAC-seq data. In the PCA plot, tTregs showed fewer changes after activation compared to Tconvs, while iTregs were closer to activated Tconv cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq PCA analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Tconvs became more accessible in 'Activation Region' after activation, with a dramatic increase in the overall accessibility.
source: In differential peak heatmap clustered by cell type, Tconvs became more accessible in 'Activation Region' after activation, and with a dramatic increase in the overall accessibility (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq differential peak analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The changes of tTregs after activation are limited, with the majority of tTreg-specific accessible region not changed and the activation region opening seen in Tconvs not more accessible in tTregs.
source: However, the changes of tTregs after activation are limited, the majority of tTreg-specific accessible region, named 'Treg Region', were not changed. Also the activation region opening seen in Tconvs were not more accessible in tTregs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq differential peak analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: iTregs were highly accessible in activation region found in activated Tconvs.
source: When comparing iTregs with the others, we found iTregs were highly accessible in activation region found in activated Tconvs (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Only a few Treg-specific peaks shown in Treg region were opened in iTregs.
source: However, only a few Treg-specific peaks shown in Treg region were opened in iTregs (Figure 3C, E).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3E.

claim: Most Treg-specific peaks were opened in tTregs but showed little accessibility in iTregs.
source: For further analysis, we isolated Treg-specific peaks. It was clear that most of them were opened in tTregs but showed little accessibility in iTregs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq analysis of Treg-specific peaks shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Foxp3 and Ctla4, expressed in both tTregs and iTregs, show high accessibility in resting and activated tTregs, but were closed or only partially opened in iTregs.
source: For example, Foxp3 and Ctla4, expressed in both tTregs and iTregs, show high accessibility in resting and activated tTregs, but were closed or only partially opened in iTregs (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by genomic track visualization of chromatin accessibility shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Genes related to inflammation cytokine in T helper cells, such as Ifng, Il4, Il17ra, and Il21, were highly opened in iTregs.
source: In contrast, genes related to inflammation cytokine in T helper cells, such as Ifng, Il4, Il17ra, and Il21, were highly opened in iTregs (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by genomic track visualization of chromatin accessibility shown in Figure 3F.

claim: At the gene expression level, iTregs have acquired some Treg features, but the chromatin accessibility was mostly trapped in activated Tconv state.
source: Overall, we showed that at the gene expression level, iTregs have acquired some Treg features, but the chromatin accessibility was mostly trapped in activated Tconv state, not only with regard to the closed Treg genes, but also with genes associated with T activation and inflammation highly opened.
evidence: Inferred from the combined RNA-seq and ATAC-seq analyses presented.

claim: Inhibition of calcium or NFAT rescued the Foxp3 expression in iTregs upon restimulation.
source: To further validate the role of calcium and NFAT in iTreg instability, we used inhibitors cyclosporine A (CsA) and CM-4620 to suppress calcium signal and NFAT, respectively. We found that inhibition of calcium or NFAT rescued the Foxp3 expression in iTregs upon restimulation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using CsA and CM-4620 shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Another SOCE inhibitor BTP2 was also verified to rescue Foxp3 expression in iTregs.
source: Another SOCE inhibitor BTP2 was also verified (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ionomycin, which can directly induce calcium release independent of TCR activation, also lead to iTreg instability.
source: Accordingly, ionomycin, which can directly induce calcium release independent of TCR activation, also lead to iTreg instability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Inhibition of NF-κB, c-Jun, or a c-Jun/c-Fos complex had no discernable effect on iTreg stability, or in one case, possibly further reduction in stability.
source: As control, inhibition of NF-κB (BAY 11-7082), c-Jun (SP600125), or a c-Jun/c-Fos complex (T5224) had no discernable effect, or in one case, possibly further reduction in stability (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: iTregs upon restimulation showed significant differences from the resting state at the transcriptome level, and this difference could be substantially reduced with inhibition of calcium or NFAT.
source: From the differential gene expression and PCA, we found that iTregs upon restimulation showed significant differences from the resting state at the transcriptome level, and this difference could be substantially reduced with inhibition of calcium or NFAT (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Calcium/NFAT-blocked iTregs were significantly closer to the resting state than the unstable ones in PCA analysis.
source: As shown in the PCA plot, calcium/NFAT-blocked iTregs were significantly closer to the resting state than the unstable ones (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The large overlap (about 80%) of genes that were rescued by CM-4620 and by CsA further supported that calcium signaling change the fate of iTregs mainly through NFAT.
source: In addition, the large overlap (about 80%) of genes that were rescued by CM-4620 and by CsA further supported that calcium signaling change the fate of iTregs mainly through NFAT (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Several genes critical for functions and stability of Tregs, such as Foxp3, Id3, Il10rb, Sema4a, Tgfbr1/2, Ms4a4b, and Nlrp6, were downregulated upon restimulation and the downregulation was blocked by inhibition of calcium and NFAT.
source: Among these genes, several of them are critical for functions and stability of Tregs, such as Foxp3, Id3, Il10rb, Sema4a, Tgfbr1/2, Ms4a4b, and Nlrp6 (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Rap-1 pathway, PD-1/PD-L1 pathway and Foxo pathway were significantly enriched among genes downregulated by NFAT.
source: In the functional analysis of these genes, we found that Rap-1 pathway, PD-1/PD-L1 pathway and Foxo pathway were significantly enriched (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Many genes associated with T helper differentiation and T cell activation, such as Il21, Il12rb2, Tbx21, Gzma, Stat2, Stat3, Atf3, and Fasl, were upregulated after restimulation but failed to do so with CM-4620 or CsA.
source: In these genes, many of them are associated with T helper differentiation and T cell activation, such as Il21, Il12rb2, Tbx21, Gzma, Stat2, Stat3, Atf3, and Fasl (Figure 4B, F).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and 4F.

claim: Th17 related pathway and Th1/Th2 related pathways were enriched among genes upregulated by NFAT.
source: Functional enrichment analysis of these upregulated genes pointed to Th17 related pathway and Th1/Th2 related pathways (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The number of NFAT peaks in restimulated iTregs was significantly higher than that in resting state.
source: The number of NFAT peaks in restimulated iTregs was significantly higher than that in resting state, which was consistent with the massive nuclear translocation of NFAT indicated by western blot (Figure 5B and Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Cut&Tag peak analysis shown in Figure 5B and western blot data in Figure 2D.

claim: NFAT peaks both before and after restimulation were enriched at promoters/transcription start site (TSS) and the first introns of genes.
source: For peak distribution at gene body, NFAT peaks both before and after restimulation were enriched at promoters/transcription start site (TSS) and the first introns of genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NFAT-upregulated TH genes were significantly more accessible in iTregs than in tTregs and Tconvs.
source: For those upregulated TH genes, we speculated that this may be associated with the highly 'activated' chromatin state of iTregs mentioned earlier. Therefore, we first checked the chromatin accessibility around the TSS in those genes and found that this group of genes was significantly more accessible in iTregs than in tTregs and Tconvs (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Il21, Il12rb2, and Tbx21 were more open in iTregs, even more so than the activated Tconvs.
source: As shown in the genome browser view, Il21, Il12rb2, and Tbx21 were more open in iTregs, even more so than the activated Tconvs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by genome track visualization shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NFAT significantly increased their binding to the TSS regions on upregulated Th genes after restimulation.
source: Further analysis revealed that NFAT significantly increased their binding to the TSS regions on upregulated Th genes after restimulation (Figure 5D), while showing little change on downregulated Treg genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by Cut&Tag analysis shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: After activation, NFAT accumulated at the sites that were prime-opened resulting in increased expression of Il21, Tbx21, and Il12rb2.
source: As shown by Il21, Tbx21, and Il12rb2, after activation, NFAT accumulated at the sites that were prime-opened resulting in their increased expression (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by genome track visualization combining NFAT binding and chromatin accessibility shown in Figure 5E.

claim: NFAT is essential to the development of tTregs.
source: As one potential counter argument, NFAT is ostensibly essential to the development of tTregs (Li et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Li et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2010).

claim: In the induction of iTregs, NFAT in collaboration with SMAD is critical.
source: In the induction of iTregs, NFAT in collaboration with SMAD is also critical (Vaeth et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2010; Tone et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Vaeth et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2010; Tone et al., 2008).

claim: Putative BATF, AP-1(Fos/Jun), and RORg-binding sites were highly enriched in restimulation state specific regions.
source: To resolve those seemingly contradictory regulations, we performed NFAT motif enrichment analysis. The results showed that putative BATF, AP-1(Fos/Jun), and RORg-binding sites were highly enriched in restimulation state specific regions (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SMAD family tended to bind to genes that were downregulated by NFAT, while AP-1 and RORg preferred binding to genes that were upregulated by NFAT.
source: For the preference of different cofactors to different gene subsets, SMAD family tended to bind to genes that were downregulated by NFAT, for example, Foxp3, while AP-1 and RORg preferred binding to genes that were upregulated by NFAT, such as TH genes (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by motif occurrence analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Upon restimulation of iTregs, NFAT prefers to cooperate with AP-1/RORg to promote the expression of prime-opened TH gene expression, and at the same time denies the SMAD programming that may be critical to maintain Treg functions and stabilities.
source: Taken together, our results appear to suggest that upon restimulation of iTregs, NFAT prefers to cooperate with AP-1/RORg to promote the expression of prime-opened TH gene expression, and at the same time denies the SMAD programming that may be critical to maintain Treg functions and stabilities.
evidence: Inferred from the motif enrichment and gene expression analyses.

claim: tTreg did not secrete IL-21 regardless of activation status, while iTreg did not secrete IL-21 at resting state but they did so after 48 hr of restimulation.
source: As shown in Figure 5H, tTreg did not secrete IL-21 regardless of activation status (undetectable), while iTreg did not secrete IL-21 at resting state but they did so after 48 hr of restimulation (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The secretion of IL-21 was inhibited by CsA and CM-4620 treatment.
source: The secretion of IL-21 was inhibited by CsA and CM-4620 treatment.
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements mentioned in the context of Figure 5H.

claim: The mutated ORAI reduced the SOCE signaling by about a half.
source: As expected, the mutated ORAI reduced the SOCE signaling by about a half (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by calcium flux measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: DN-ORAI expressing iTregs showed stronger stability with higher retention of Foxp3 than WT-ORAI iTregs upon restimulation.
source: When we restimulated this DN-ORAI expressing iTregs with anti-CD3/CD28, they showed stronger stability with higher retention of Foxp3 than WT-ORAI iTregs (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by Foxp3 expression analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: DN-ORAI iTregs displayed more potent suppressive activity than control iTreg in in vitro suppression assay.
source: Consistently, DN-ORAI iTregs displayed more potent suppressive activity than control iTreg in in vitro suppression assay (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by suppression assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: DN-ORAI iTregs were more resistant to the loss of Foxp3 and thus were more stable than control WT-ORAI iTregs in vivo.
source: Analysis of the percentage of Foxp3+ cells in mLN 5 days after adoptive transfer showed that DN-ORAI iTregs were more resistant to the loss of Foxp3 and thus were more stable than control WT-ORAI iTregs (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo adoptive transfer experiment shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Rapamycin and AS tended to close the activation region in iTregs.
source: Our findings revealed that rapamycin and AS tended to close the activation region (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), while Vc, removal of CD28, and AS increased the accessibility of Treg genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Vitamin C, removal of CD28, and AS increased the accessibility of Treg genes in iTregs.
source: Our findings revealed that rapamycin and AS tended to close the activation region (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), while Vc, removal of CD28, and AS increased the accessibility of Treg genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The stability of tTregs is established prior to their exit from the thymus.
source: The stability of tTregs is established prior to their exit from the thymus (Ohkura et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohkura et al., 2013.

claim: In the thymus, Foxp3 works with other transcription factors, such as NFAT and c-Rel to maintain a steady transcriptional program.
source: In the thymus, Foxp3 works with other transcription factors, such as NFAT and c-Rel to maintain a steady transcriptional program (Fu et al., 2012; Hill et al., 2007; Samstein et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Fu et al., 2012; Hill et al., 2007; Samstein et al., 2012).

claim: The extensive demethylation of Foxp3 CNS2 is critical to tTreg stable phenotype, an event likely taking place before Foxp3 expression.
source: At the same time, the extensive demethylation of Foxp3 CNS2 is also critical to their stable phenotype, an event likely taking place before Foxp3 expression (Samstein et al., 2012; Ohkura et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Samstein et al., 2012; Ohkura et al., 2012).

claim: Induced Tregs use a different program that relies on the binding of SMADs to the CNS1 region to initiate Foxp3 expression.
source: Induced Tregs, on the other hand, use a different program that relies on the binding of SMADs to the CNS1 region to initiate Foxp3 expression (Tone et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tone et al., 2008.

claim: This SMAD binding mediated transcription is dependent on Foxp3 H3K4me3 modification.
source: This SMAD binding mediated transcription is dependent on Foxp3 H3K4me3 modification.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the context of discussing iTreg induction mechanisms.

claim: In the absence of SMAD, H3K4me3 is partially lost, resulting in iTreg phenotypical shift.
source: In the absence of SMAD, H3K4me3 is partially lost, resulting in iTreg phenotypical shift (Tone et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tone et al., 2008.

claim: iTregs do not immediately lose Foxp3 expression upon TGF-β withdrawal, the loss of Foxp3 is evident hours or days after TCR signaling.
source: Withstanding this paradigm, iTregs do not immediately lose Foxp3 expression upon TGF-β withdrawal, the loss of Foxp3 is evident hours or days after TCR signaling (Selvaraj and Geiger, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Selvaraj and Geiger, 2007.

claim: While the epigenetic alterations are necessary, an activation event is required to drive the loss of phenotype in iTregs.
source: This indicates that while the epigenetic alterations are necessary, an activation event is required to drive the loss of phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that iTregs lose Foxp3 after TCR signaling rather than immediately upon TGF-β withdrawal.

claim: tTregs utilize both truncated calcium signal and conserved chromatin accessibility to systematically reduce their TCR responsiveness, ensuring their stability.
source: We observed differences between tTregs and iTregs in calcium signal and Th gene accessibility. tTregs utilize both truncated calcium signal and conserved chromatin accessibility to systematically reduce their TCR responsiveness, ensuring their stability.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of calcium signaling and chromatin accessibility differences.

claim: In iTregs, sustained Ca2+ signal leads to strong NFAT activation, which with the help of cofactors causes high expression of TH genes, leading to instability.
source: In contrast, iTregs retain the full strength of the TCR signaling, particularly the sustained vibration of SOCE signal, the key factor that drives NFAT synthesis and nuclear translocation. With the help of several cofactors, such as AP-1, NFAT caused the high expression of these TH genes, which subsequently subverts the original differentiation of iTregs, leading to their instability.
evidence: Inferred from the combined observations of SOCE, NFAT translocation, and gene expression changes.

claim: Direct inhibition of SOCE signaling and NFAT can enhance iTreg stability in vitro and in vivo.
source: Direct inhibition of SOCE signaling and NFAT can enhance iTreg stability in vitro and in vivo (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using inhibitors and DN-ORAI, summarized in the proposed model in Figure 6E.

claim: Inhibition of NFAT by low-dose CsA increased the number of tTreg in atopic dermatitis patients.
source: Nevertheless, in line with our results, inhibition of NFAT by low-dose CsA increased the number of tTreg in atopic dermatitis patients (Brandt et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brandt et al., 2009.

claim: There is an inverse association between SOCE signal and Treg stability.
source: It seems reasonable to establish an inverse association between SOCE signal and Treg stability.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observations showing that reduced SOCE enhances stability while sustained SOCE reduces it.

claim: In contrast to Tconvs and iTregs, there must be a negative signal loop that blunts SOCE vibration in tTregs.
source: However, in contrast to Tconvs and iTregs, there must be a negative signal loop that blunts SOCE vibration in tTregs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SOCE is truncated in tTregs but not in iTregs or Tconvs.

claim: Treg-specific hypomethylation is crucial for tTregs to stably express their Treg-specific genes.
source: Our results are consistent with the understanding that Treg-specific hypomethylation is crucial for tTregs to stably express their Treg-specific genes (Samstein et al., 2012; Ohkura et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Samstein et al., 2012; Ohkura et al., 2012) and consistency with current results.

claim: Epigenetic changes related to Treg-specific genes are mostly absent in iTregs, resulting in their instability.
source: Those epigenetic changes are mostly absent in iTregs, resulting in their instability.
evidence: Inferred from the ATAC-seq data showing closed Treg-specific regions in iTregs.

claim: Current treatments such as vitamin C and CD28 blockage applied to achieve demethylation and accessibility of Treg genes in iTregs are worthy attempts.
source: Therefore, current treatments such as vitamin C and CD28 blockage applied to achieve demethylation and accessibility of Treg genes in iTregs are worthy attempts (Mikami et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Mikami et al., 2020; Yue et al., 2016) and consistency with current findings.

claim: There are a cluster of activation and differentiation-related peaks present in iTregs that remain silent in tTregs upon TCR stimulation.
source: However, our work indicates that at least in ATAC-seq analyses, there are a cluster of activation and differentiation-related peaks present in iTregs that remain silent in tTregs upon TCR stimulation.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data showing open activation regions in iTregs but not in tTregs.

claim: These activation peaks were targeted by abundant NFAT in the iTreg nuclei following activation, leading to the upregulation of Th genes.
source: Critically, these peaks were targeted by abundant NFAT in the iTreg nuclei following activation, leading to the upregulation of Th genes.
evidence: Supported by Cut&Tag data showing NFAT binding to open activation regions.

claim: Producing highly stable iTregs would likely require a combined approach to demethylate Treg-specific genes and at the same time to block the activation and differentiation-related genes.
